report search limits instead of assuming every workflow reaches the function.

touched by the task diff or its changed data flow, inspect the task tree to
determine whether the defect persists.

do not let a focused task diff silently imply that inherited code can return
or otherwise operate successfully.

parent trees to find the code that reads the data back. Compare the writer's
and reader's resolved locations, inspect which parent directories are created,
and leave unexecuted filesystem-library behavior explicitly unestablished.

how far an import-time failure reaches. If the explanation depends on a
language or library version fact, cite eligible documentation supplied in the
evidence catalog or state that the version fact is unestablished.

parent tree for the exact key and plausible near spellings. Inspect the task
diff and relevant consumers before describing the key's effect; do not infer
the intended spelling from the helper or variable name alone.

whole parent tree, including tests and utilities, for every builder of that
dictionary and every caller of the function. Inspect each relevant construction
site; a search limited to the implementation package cannot establish caller
compatibility.
When a documentation change describes command-line options, defaults or runtime
behavior, check every documented statement against the parser and relevant
consumers, not only statements that initially appear suspicious. Record loose
or unsupported claims and distinguish source inspection from execution.
When the commit message names a platform, product or error, search the whole
parent tree for that term before concluding that no in-scope source bears on it.
Report related occurrences without assuming they describe the same defect.

a run result supports the claim. This is an authoring-boundary candidate, not a
request to publish or mark an entry reviewed.

The path hints are navigation derived from cutoff-bound issue text, not evidence; read the item before using it. Report the item's own title and framing faithfully. Label every link you draw to the task as inference and state the concrete matching basis, such as a traceback line matching a source line.

Report what their own limits, tiers or preconditions show, as source inspection. State a conclusion about the author's reason as inference, and say that the rationale is unestablished only after that inspection.

Adds or changes means the task diff registers that architecture or modifies its model or configuration class. This applies to configuration files only; read tensor headers as needed to support claims.

These are navigation hints, not established relationships; fetch bodies with web_fetch, page with evidence_index(index_id="closed_discussions"), label task links as inference with their concrete basis, and report each item’s own title and framing faithfully.

find that commit's entry with the ancestor tools and read it before finalizing. Say which entries you read and
what they establish about the code the task relies on, including any guard, precondition or recorded defect; if
you read none, say so.

When one commit makes several edits, check whether any of them supplies a precondition another needs before
describing them as independent.

When the task starts calling an existing function, method or mechanism from a place that did not call it before,

the new call omits and state what the inspected code would do without it. If there are no other callers, say so.

call path that reaches the unguarded case, report it under findings as suspected, with its limits; do not leave

When the task adds or changes a model architecture, or code that names checkpoint tensors or depends on their

reads. Check every tensor name the code requests, including alternate and optional names, against the names in
the header, and say which are absent and which path the code then takes. Do not describe tensor layout as
unestablished while headers are available and unread.

from exllamav3.util.progress import ProgressBar
from PIL import Image
import glob
from pathlib import (Path)
from imgsearch_gallery import gallery

"""
Small example of using a VLM to query multiple images with the same yes/no question and collect all the positive
results. Note that only Gemma3 currently benefits from batch sizes higher than 1. The model is only sampled for one
token per image and only the relative probabilities of 'Yes' and 'No' are considered. A more advanced pipeline is
probably required to take full advantage of most models.

Example:

python examples/imgsearch.py /path/to/images -m /path/to/vlm -v -p "Are there any cats in this image?" 
"""

def resolve_files(input_path):
    input_path = Path(input_path)
    if input_path.is_dir():
        return [str(p) for p in input_path.rglob("*") if p.is_file()]
    elif input_path.is_file():
        return [str(input_path)]
    else:
        return [str(p) for p in glob.glob(str(input_path), recursive = True) if Path(p).is_file()]

def get_token_mask(tokenizer, substr):
    vocab = tokenizer.get_id_to_piece_list()
    substr1 = substr.upper()
    substr2 = substr.upper()
    mask = torch.tensor([(token.upper().startswith(substr1) or token.upper().startswith(substr2)) for token in vocab])
    return mask

@torch.inference_mode()
def main(args):

    # Resolve filenames
    input_files = []
    for arg in args.input:
        input_files += resolve_files(arg)

    # Prepare model etc.
    model, config, _, tokenizer = model_init.init(args)

    # Load the image component model
    vision_model = Model.from_config(config, component = "vision")
    vision_model.load(progressbar = True)

    batchsize = args.batchsize
    if batchsize > 1 and not vision_model.caps.get("fixed_size_image_embeddings"):
        print(" !! Cannot do batched image ingestion with this model, falling back to batch size 1")
        batchsize = 1

    # Output masks
    yes_mask = get_token_mask(tokenizer, "yes")
    no_mask = get_token_mask(tokenizer, "no")
    vocab_size = tokenizer.actual_vocab_size  # To account for padded logits

    # Results
    skipped_files = 0
    total_files = 0
    all_matches = []

    # Process images

{"ok": true, "result": {"offset": 0, "next_offset": 7404, "truncated": false, "text": "{
  "discussion": {
    "author_login": "meigami0",
    "created_at": "2025-06-09T10:03:09Z",
    "kind": "issue",
    "number": 50,
    "state": "OPEN",
    "title": "RuntimeError: Insufficient VRAM in split for model and cache despite remaining 1GB VRAM (exllamav3 + tabbyAPI)",
    "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/50"
  },
  "objects": [
    {
      "author_login": "meigami0",
      "content": "I encountered a VRAM allocation issue while testing exllamav3 quantized models with TabbyAPI. Even with ~1GB VRAM remaining, the system throws an error: `RuntimeError: Insufficient VRAM in split for model and cache`. Below are test results for two models on 24564MiB VRAM (RTX4090):  \n\n#### Model 1: **Nemotron-Super-49B** (3.0bpw, `cache-mode FP16`)  \n- 2k context: 19162MiB used  \n- 12k context: 21342MiB used  \n- 20k context: 23094MiB used  \n- 21k context: 23194MiB used  \n- 22k context: OOM  \n\n#### Model 2: **gemma3-27b** (5.0bpw, `cache-mode Q6`)  \n- 2k context: 17404MiB used  \n- 12k context: 19404MiB used  \n- 22k context: 21660MiB used  \n- 30k context: 23238MiB used  \n- 31k context: OOM  \n\nEnvironment: WSL Ubuntu+Python12+torch2.7.0+cu128+exllamav3-0.0.3+tabbyAPI default config\n\n**Questions:**  \n- Is this behavior expected under exllamav3\u2019s current memory management design?  \n- Are there recommended configurations or workarounds to better utilize the remaining VRAM?",
      "content_sha256": "38c73221713b41d0e3eb99acbaccdcbf2e804689c2fdbf9d48e8726b20590df7",
      "created_at": "2025-06-09T10:03:09Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-06-09T10:03:09Z",
      "source_id": "I_kwDOOU24Gs66jTPW",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/50"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "A couple of likely contributing reasons:\n\nMomentary VRAM allocations can be so quick that they don't show up in a monitoring utility which might be polling, say, once per second. So if you see:\n     \n- 20k context uses 23.1 GB, and\n- 21k context uses 23.2 GB, so you might expect\n- 22k context uses 23.3 GB, but..\n\n... this might not be accounting for 0.75 GB of temporary storage for some large operation that's too fast to notice.\n\nThe reason you might get this OoM error while loading is that the model performs a dummy forward pass as it shovels tensors onto the GPU, to determine precisely where the overflow occurs and thus where it should split the model in a multi-GPU setup.\n\nThis inference-while-loading can make it look like the model needs more VRAM as it's loading than it does afterwards. Really it's just accounting for the worst case while loading. The chunk size is adjustable in Tabby's config if you want a different worst case. Smaller chunk size reduces the overall VRAM requirement somewhat but also makes prefill somewhat slower. Tabby's default is 2048.\n\nAlso, by default a small buffer amount is reserved on each GPU to keep things stable, especially for the first GPU which might also be running a desktop environment. You can change the size of this reserve in Tabby's config, or if you're calling ExLlama directly, there are arguments to the `load()` and `load_gen()` functions.\n\nIn multi-GPU splits, ExLlama only splits whole layers. So if each of your devices would fit 12.7 layers in theory, you end up with 12 layers on each and 0.7 layers worth of unused memory.\n\nFinally, VRAM fragmentation is a thing and is not accounted for by `nvidia-smi`. Having 23.5 GB free on a 24 GB device doesn't mean you can allocate an extra block of 0.5 GB tensor somewhere.",
      "content_sha256": "28a15bca9278573b5bf3cd2205cecc8bf1f5835e2960b26c0502508d8edb06bc",
      "created_at": "2025-06-11T12:27:11Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-06-11T12:29:18Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6wlA8k",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/50#issuecomment-2962493220"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "Vhallo",
      "content": "There may be something strange going on with EXL3's VRAM utilization. Encountered the \"RuntimeError\" error testing some edge cases with some free VRAM left over. However, while a single 256 context step was impossible, raising the Chunk Size from 256 to the max of 4096 worked fine. Seems a bit strange, and could indicate an issue?\n\nYou also mentioned the autosplit_reserve. Is that supposed to do anything with a single GPU? (Setting it to 0 / absurdly high in Tabby's config as a test had no impact at least.)",
      "content_sha256": "4a0618df0d1017e9e016bf81f5d912c3117b7b46bd1756f0b45ee13c9e8c0cbd",
      "created_at": "2025-06-12T00:48:04Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-06-12T00:48:04Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6wtPPI",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/50#issuecomment-2964648904"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "Vhallo",
      "content": "Turns out even with CUDA sysmem fallback set to \"prefer no sysmem fallback\", it can still end up using some sysmem when changing Chunk Size, with slightly degraded performance. Doesn't seem to happen with context though strangely enough.",
      "content_sha256": "cf69675e1f659bbfdd4374af33f769be7591a81f3278401ff39b7b471112e35b",
      "created_at": "2025-06-12T21:29:03Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-06-12T21:29:03Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6w6zK1",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/50#issuecomment-2968203957"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "It does affect single-GPU setups, and is especially important there since you'll run into trouble if you allocate 100% of your VRAM and then try to do anything in a desktop environment.\n\nMemory management in Windows is always problematic, though. It could be a complication in that regard, or maybe some confusion caused by WSL?  What happens if you try to run Tabby/ExLlama natively in Windows?",
      "content_sha256": "8617c8b45d1ff057364e1e3dfd40a48c6f79b4ec2fa819da18ce5cf9acd4d6df",
      "created_at": "2025-06-14T15:47:05Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-06-14T15:47:05Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6xMfZn",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/50#issuecomment-2972841575"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "Vhallo",
      "content": "That already was native Windows (10) in my case. But I looked into it, and autosplit_reserve doesn't seem to work with a single GPU in Tabby because the following check in TabbyAPI\\backends\\exllamav3\\model.py:\n```\n        # Set GPU split options\n        if gpu_count == 1:\n            self.gpu_split_auto = False\n            logger.info(\"Disabling GPU split because one GPU is in use.\")\n        else:\n        ...\n```\n\nChanging gpu_count to 0 for testing seems to make autosplit_reserve work, as it loads fine normally and then fails as expected when setting autosplit_reserve to a high value.",
      "content_sha256": "ca6fc0f80014cb0b0177130a5e140c9f7514e1ac3883ebc44aee6b2151393c49",
      "created_at": "2025-06-14T16:51:55Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-06-14T16:51:55Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6xMmOb",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/50#issuecomment-2972869531"
    }
  ]
}
